title: Accountability in U.S. Foreign Policy
text:
This post is a placeholder for a future project.
There seems to be a lack of accountability in U.S. foreign policy. Was anyone held responsible for the 2003 invasion of Iraq?
Professions develop accountability mechanisms all the time. Doctors have to maintain their license. Lawyers can be disbarred. Why isn’t there something similar in foreign policy? It may be helpful to distinguish between politicians, foreign service, and ‘thought leaders’.
Is there anything to be learned from other countries? There are many examples of other democracies holding leaders accountable for their actions, but are any of them due to foreign policy?

title: About
text:
My name is Thomas Scherer. I have worked in government at the US Institute of Peace, academia at the University of California, San Diego, non-profits at the think tank fp21, and media at Bloomberg Economics. I am a volunteer firefighter, gamer, and husky dad. I earned a PhD in international relations from Princeton University.
I am the author of AbroadReview, a living literature review on topics in foreign policy and international relations (also available on Beehiiv and Substack). It’s goal is to provide a clear perspective on world events based on theories and evidence from international relations academic research.
AI usage: No AI is used in any writing on this website, just Grammarly. I have used Gemini to assist with coding in Quarto and R for creating the website.

About the website
This website is built on Quarto and hosted on Github. It was widely adapted from a template by Dr. Gang He.

title: The Cap Times hawks timely debt alarmism
text:
Politics, like some birds, follow migration patterns. As the electoral seasons turn, you can expect to see certain species that you haven’t seen in a while. Before an election, ‘border birds’ fly through with their caws warning of migratory caravans. They move rather quickly and are often gone as soon as the election is over.
The deficit hawk’s migration pattern is less regular but just as predictable. They can disappear for years, but once democrats take power, they reappear and hunker down until Republicans retake control. Just weeks after the 2026 blue wave election, hawkish Senator Grassley (IA-R) has returned to warn of the “stunning” federal debt. Although Grassleys have perched in the Senate since 1981, you can identify a deficit-hawk Grassley by its distinctive song. The newly arrived hawkish Grassley gives a shrill scream about deficits, while the Grassley seen in 2001 passed $1.35 trillion in tax cuts and was spotted in 2025 spearheading large portions of the $3.4 trillion Big Beautiful Bill Act with nary a fiscal peep.



Figure: Bluesky birders rejoice at the return of the Deficit-Warbling Grassley


Today I saw reports of a debt hawk singing right here in Madison! The Concord Coalition is giving a series of talks, noteworthy enough to get a front-page mention and a full op-ed by Cap Times President and Publisher Paul Fanlund titled “Why the national debt should be a progressive priority.”
But is this really a cynical deficit hawk? Concord Coalition’s speaker and president, Carolyn Bourdeaux, is a former Democratic representative and will be flanked by two former Wisconsin congressmen, Rob Kind (D) and Reid Ribble (R).
I do not know what is motivating Bourdeaux, Kind, or even Fanlund to draw attention to the deficit in this moment. Maybe they are truly concerned about the federal debt and believe their efforts are better spent targeting the left because they know the right doesn’t actually care about such things.
What I do know is that the Concord Coalition’s is supported by the Concord Coalition Corp, whose largest donor by far is the Peter G Peterson Foundation, and by the Concord Coalition Action Fund, which received a large grant from the Peterson Solutions Fund.
The Peterson Foundation was founded by Peter Peterson, a cabinet member under President Nixon. Peterson has been criticized for using the foundation for his ultimate goal of gutting Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, while simultaneously opposing deficit-cutting measures that would affect him.
The Peterson Solution Fund is currently led by Executive Director Brett Loper, a former American Express executive and staffer to House Speakers Boehner (R) and DeLay (R). Loper reportedly had a bit part in the Abramoff scandal, accompanying another DeLay staffer to find pork opportunities on the Marianas islands to support Abramoff’s favored politicians.
When the newly elected class joins the U.S. Congress in January, they will have many voter concerns to address: healthcare, gas prices, corruption, an economy hobbled by tariffs and war. And yet, here is the Concord Coalition, abetted by Capital Times, calling out the importance of the national debt, a call oft heard once (and almost exclusively when) democrats gain power.
In the age of algorithms, we must be wary of what we are being served and how it got there. In this case, the money trail leads to some big money actors with questionable motives. This is not to say the national debt is not an issue, nor is it to cast aspersions on Bourdeaux, Kind, or Fanlund. This talk is happening not because it is a top priority for Americans, but because Republican operators Peter Peterson and Brett Loper want to make sure you hear their song. As Congress’s leaves turn blue with the changing of the political seasons, we will surely be hearing such songs often as the deficit hawks return.
